subject: Banking
title: The Knights Templar Bank
description: A fast breakdown of The Knights Templar Bank for builders.

hook.text: The Knights Templar ran medieval Europe's first international bank.

buildup.text: Pilgrims carried letters of credit instead of gold. A Templar note in London was honored in the Holy Land.

discovery.text: The Templars invented branch banking and foreign exchange. Their network spanned England, France, and the Middle East.

twist.text: King Philip IV of France owed the Templars a fortune. He arrested them, seized their assets, and dissolved the order.

climax.text: The Templars proved that banking creates power. And that power threatened kings who owed bankers too much money.

punchline.text: Templars built banking. A king who owed them money destroyed them.

quiz.question: Why did King Philip IV destroy the Knights Templar?
options: He owed them money and wanted to seize their wealth

details.summary: The Knights Templar operated one of the first international banking networks during the Crusades, offering safe deposit, long-distance fund transfer, and credit services across Europe and the Middle East from the 12th to 14th centuries.
details.whyItMatters: The Templars solved the critical problem of moving money safely across continents. Their banking innovations enabled international commerce and pilgrimage, creating financial infrastructure that prefigured modern international banking.
takeaways: Pilgrims deposited money in London and withdrew it in Jerusalem
The Templars managed finances for kings and the papacy
King Philip IV of France destroyed the order in 1307, partly to seize their wealth

faq.question: How did the Templars' banking system work?
faq.answer: A pilgrim could deposit gold at a Templar preceptory in Europe and receive a letter of credit. Upon arriving in the Holy Land, they presented the letter and received the equivalent in local currency, minus a fee for the service.

faq.question: Was the Templars' banking their real power?
faq.answer: Their financial power became more significant than their military role. By managing royal treasuries and lending to monarchs, they became so powerful that King Philip IV of France orchestrated their arrest partly to seize assets and cancel his debts.
